title: Hold a wine bottle in its cradle by the neck with one hand while the other uncorks it with a corkscrew
instruction: Hold the wine bottle by its neck with one hand, and with the other screw the corkscrew into the cork and pull the cork out of the bottle.
context: Opening wine at the table is routine work for waiters and sommeliers: one hand steadies the bottle while the other drives the corkscrew in and draws the cork, which takes a firm pull. A bottle in a pouring cradle is not held by the cradle against that pull.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed wooden pouring cradle: two slats under the bottle's body, on two posts, on a base board 9 x 22 cm on the table. (2) A loose 75 cl wine bottle, dark green glass, 1.2 kg: a body 7.5 cm across and 20 cm long, a shoulder, and a neck 3.1 cm across and 9 cm long (bore 2.4 cm) ending in a lip 3.5 cm across. It lies in the cradle along the left-right line 27 cm forward, tipped up 15 degrees, its neck toward the right; the middle of its mouth is on the centre line, 12.5 cm above the table. (3) A loose cork in the neck, 2.3 cm across and 4 cm long, its outer face flush with the lip. (4) A loose corkscrew, 60 g: a round wooden knob 2 cm across and 3 cm long, a steel shank 1.5 cm long and a worm 0.7 cm across and 4.5 cm long to its point. It stands knob up in a fixed dark stand (a base 4 x 4 cm and a square tube 1.2 cm wide, 7 cm tall) 25 cm forward, 18 cm right of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The corkscrew catches in the cork when its point is 1 to 12 mm into the cork's face, within 6 mm of its middle and lined up within 12 degrees, and it is turned a quarter turn clockwise (seen from its knob); turns count net from then. Out: the cork drawn at least 4.5 cm out of the neck (its inner end 5 mm past the lip). In its cradle: the bottle moved no more than 2 cm and turned no more than 5 degrees from where it lay. 1.0: the cork out on the caught corkscrew and the bottle in its cradle; 0.5: the corkscrew caught and turned at least one turn in; 0.25: caught; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held with the bottle still for 1 s.
reset_notes: Unscrew the cork from the corkscrew and push it back into the neck flush with the lip; stand the corkscrew back in its stand and lay the bottle back in the cradle.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the worm is a plain rod; its thread is a joint switched on once it catches, which keeps the cork on its axis, drags and draws the cork 12 mm along per turn. The cork is a solid plug held in the neck by a spring that gives way at 12 N and keeps it where it is pulled to; worm and cork, and cork and bottle, do not collide. No wine. Cradle and stand are fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
